publish.title: How to Tell if a Crypto Website Is Legit or a Scam (8 Checks)
publish.description:
How do you tell if a crypto website or app is legit or a scam? In this beginner guide: how clone sites copy real exchanges with lookalike addresses and sponsored search ads, how fake wallet apps get into app stores, and how fake trading platforms show made-up profits and then charge "taxes" to withdraw. You'll get 8 simple checks, from domain age and registration lookups to the one rule that stops the withdrawal-fee trap.

{chapters}

This video is for educational purposes only and is not financial advice.

#cryptoscam #crypto #cryptoforbeginners

scenes.name: hook
narration: Maria wanted to check her crypto balance, so she searched for her exchange.
She clicked the first result. Same logo, same colors, same login page.
She typed her password and her two-factor code.
Ten minutes later, her account was empty. Every coin had gone to a stranger.
The site was a copy, and its address was off by one letter.
In this video, you'll learn how to tell if a crypto website or app is legit or a scam, with eight checks that take about five minutes.

widgets.title: Withdrawal sent
widgets.sub: All funds to a new address

elements.sub: 8 checks for any crypto website or app

scenes.name: why
narration: Here's why this matters.
The FBI's crime complaint center logged more than eleven billion dollars in reported crypto fraud losses in 2025.
Over seven billion of that came from fake investment schemes.
Fake crypto sites come in two kinds.
The first is a clone: a copy of a real exchange, built to steal your login.
The second is a fake platform: an exchange or investment site that only shows you made-up numbers.
Let's start with the clones, because they can empty an account in minutes.

elements.text: Clones first: they work in minutes

scenes.name: step1-address
narration: Step one: read the address, letter by letter.
Scammers register names that look almost right.
CryptoApp, but with a zero instead of the letter O.
The real name, plus a dash and the word login.
Or dot co, instead of dot com.
On a phone, the address bar is tiny, and your eyes see what they expect to see.
And the padlock icon doesn't help. It only means the connection is encrypted, not that the site is honest.
Scam sites get a padlock for free, just like real ones.
So always read the address itself, not the little lock next to it.

elements.title: Read the address letter by letter

elements.text: A padlock is not a safety badge

scenes.name: step2-source
narration: Step two: ask yourself how you got there.
Scammers buy search ads, so a fake site can sit above the real one, marked as sponsored.
They also send links by email, text and social media: your account is locked, verify now.
The fix is simple. Open the real site once, carefully, and bookmark it.
Or use the official app you already have.
From then on, never log in from an ad, a search result or a link someone sent you.
It takes two extra seconds, and it beats every fake ad on the internet.

elements.text: the fake one is on top
Never log in from an ad or a link

scenes.name: step3-apps
narration: Step three: check an app before you install it.
Fake crypto apps don't only live on shady websites.
In April 2026, researchers at Kaspersky reported twenty-six fake wallet apps on Apple's own App Store.
Some looked like games or calculators, then pushed people to install a fake wallet that stole their seed phrase.
Before you install, check the developer name, and open the store link from the company's official website.
And if an app asks you to install a profile, or to download something from outside the store, stop right there.
So far, those were copies of real companies. The next ones are harder to spot, because the whole company is fake.

items.text: Use the link on the official site

elements.text: Next: the whole company is fake

scenes.name: step4-promises
narration: Step four: look at what they promise.
Fake platforms advertise fixed daily profits, like two percent a day, guaranteed.
Many add VIP levels: deposit more, and your rate goes up.
Two percent a day sounds small. But it would double your money in about five weeks.
Real exchanges don't promise you any profit. They just let you buy and sell.
So when a site guarantees returns, the promise itself is the warning sign.
No legal investment can promise that, and no real company will try.

scenes.name: step5-registration
narration: Step five: check that the company is registered, on official websites.
In the U.S., crypto exchanges generally must register with FinCEN as a money services business.
Many states also require a license. You can look those up on NMLS Consumer Access.
And the CFTC keeps a RED list of foreign firms that solicit Americans without registering.
Never trust a certificate shown on the site itself.
Washington State regulators warned about a fake bitcoin trader license that claimed to come from the city of Seattle. No such license exists.
Registration doesn't make a company safe. But most scam platforms aren't registered anywhere.
So treat a missing registration as a stop sign, and a found one as just the first check.

scenes.name: step6-age
narration: Step six: check how old the site is, and who is behind it.
Type the address into ICANN's free lookup tool to see when the domain was created.
If a platform says it has served clients since 2015, but its domain is three weeks old, you have your answer.
Look for a real street address you can check on a map, and a phone number that a person answers.
If the only contact is a live chat or a messaging app, that's a red flag.
And search the name plus the word scam. Reviews on the site itself, and awards you've never heard of, prove nothing.
Real people describing real problems, on other sites, tell you far more.

elements.title: Check its age and who is behind it

scenes.name: step7-payment
narration: Step seven: watch how they want to be paid.
Many fake platforms won't take a bank transfer or a card.
Instead, they tell you to buy crypto on a licensed exchange, then send it to an address they give you.
That's on purpose. A crypto transfer can't be reversed. Once it leaves your wallet, it's gone.
Now let me show you how all of these signs look together, in real life.

elements.title: Watch how they want to be paid

elements.text: All the signs, in real life

scenes.name: story-alex
narration: Imagine Alex. A friendly stranger online shows him screenshots of her trading profits.
She sends him a link to a platform called CryptoTradePro.
He deposits five hundred dollars, and his balance grows every day.
He even withdraws a hundred dollars to test it. It arrives.
So he deposits twenty thousand more. A few weeks later, his balance shows forty thousand.
When he tries to withdraw, a message appears: pay a fifteen percent tax first.
He pays. Then comes an anti-money-laundering fee. Then an account upgrade fee.
The forty thousand never existed. It was just a number on a screen.
Alex lost twenty thousand five hundred dollars, plus every fee he paid.

elements.text: just a number on a screen

scenes.name: step8-fees
narration: That's step eight: never pay to get your own money out.
A real platform takes its fees from your balance.
Taxes go to the government through your own tax return, not to a support agent in a chat.
If a site says you must send more money before you can withdraw, your money is already gone.
Stop paying. Every new fee is just one more way to take more.

elements.text: Stop paying. Never pay to withdraw.

scenes.name: myth-withdrawal
narration: Myth: if I could withdraw, it must be real.
Fake platforms often let you take out a small amount, on purpose.
It costs them a hundred dollars, and it buys your trust for twenty thousand.
A small withdrawal proves nothing. A real platform lets you take out all of your money, at any time, with no surprise fees.
So don't risk money you can't afford to lose just to find out.

elements.text: Don't risk money you can't lose

scenes.name: tip-caught
narration: Tip: what to do if you think you've already been caught.
Stop sending money, no matter what fee they ask for.
If you typed your password into a fake site, change it right away in the real app, and reset your two-factor.
Report it to the FBI at ic3.gov, and to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov.
Tell your bank and your exchange too, and keep every screenshot and transaction ID.
And ignore anyone who offers to recover your money for a fee. That's usually the same scam, part two.
Real police and real exchanges never charge you upfront to get your money back.

scenes.name: recap
narration: Let's recap the eight checks.
One: read the address letter by letter. The padlock is not proof.
Two: use your bookmark, never an ad or a link.
Three: get apps through the link on the official website.
Four: guaranteed profits mean scam.
Five: look up the registration on official sites.
Six: check the domain age and the real contact details.
Seven: be careful when they only take crypto.
Eight: never pay to withdraw your own money.

scenes.name: outro
narration: If this helped, subscribe.
Next, I'll explain what a pig butchering scam is, and how crypto romance scams work.
And tell me in the comments: have you ever landed on a fake crypto site?
